en: Udāna 6.8 Gaṇikāsutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time in Rājagaha there were two factions who were infatuated with and had their hearts bound to a certain courtesan;
having come to blows, quarreling, and falling into dispute, they attacked one another with their hands, they attacked with clods of earth, they attacked with sticks, and they attacked with swords.
There they undergo even death, or suffering equal to death.
Then, a number of bhikkhus, having dressed in the morning and taking their bowls and robes, entered Rājagaha for alms.
Having walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from their almsround after the meal, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, in Rājagaha, two groups of people have become infatuated with and bound to a certain courtesan.

Having come to brawls, quarrels, and disputes, they attack one another with their hands, they attack one another with clods of earth, they attack one another with sticks, and they attack one another with swords.”
“They meet death there, or at least the suffering that is tantamount to death.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Both what has been attained and what is yet to be attained—both these are strewn with dust for one who trains while being afflicted.”
Those who take the training as their essence, whose life is devoted to rules and observances and the holy life, and who take attendance upon others as their essence—this is one extreme.
And those who speak thus:
“There is no fault in sensual pleasures”—this is the second extreme.
"Both these extremes increase the cemetery; cemeteries increase views.
Not having directly known both these extremes, some hang back, while others run too far.
But for those who have directly known them, and who neither exist therein nor designate a name for it—for them there is no round for the purpose of designation."
The eighth.
